speaker: Doctor
text: Let's start at the beginning: can you describe exactly where the pain is located and what makes it worse? REQUEST TEST: Blood work for inflammatory markers.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since your inflammatory markers are normal, this suggests the issue may not be systemic or autoimmune. Can you tell me if you notice any swelling, redness, or warmth in the affected wrist, and does the pain wake you up at night? REQUEST TEST: X-ray of the wrist.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: X-ray of the wrist shows no evidence of fracture, dislocation, or osteoarthritis. There are no visible joint effusions, calcifications, or erosions. The carpal bones appear intact with normal joint spaces.

speaker: Doctor
text: Excellent, the structural integrity of your wrist appears intact. Since inflammation is not present, do you experience any numbness, tingling, or a "pins and needles" sensation in your thumb, index, or middle fingers? REQUEST IMAGES: Ultrasound of the carpal tunnel.

speaker: Patient
text: 34-year-old female. The patient reports experiencing pain in her right thumb and wrist, which radiates to her elbow for the past three months. The pain worsens when she holds her infant son and is alleviated somewhat with an ice pack. She mentions a history of falling on her right outstretched hand about six months ago. She also notes that her mother has a history of chronic joint pain treated with methotrexate. The patient has been taking ibuprofen as needed for her symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on your history of falling on an outstretched hand and the specific radiation of pain from your thumb to your elbow, do you feel any clicking, popping, or grinding sensations when you move your thumb across your wrist? REQUEST TEST: MRI of the right wrist and thumb.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis. The normal MRI rules out internal derangement like a tendon tear or ganglion cyst, and your history of repetitive strain with thumb-to-elbow radiation is classic for inflammation of the first dorsal compartment tendons. I will perform a physical exam (Finkelstein's test) to confirm the diagnosis.
